summary: Specifies a mechanism for delivering the Attribute-Value Pairs of the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA) in encrypted form. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Messages used to prove who you are to a network could be read by snoopers. This memo lets parts of them be scrambled so only the right people read them.

questions: how does pana derive encryption keys
subtitle: How PANA lets selected attribute-value pairs travel encrypted instead of in the clear.

tldr.problem: PANA carries its payloads in attribute-value pairs (AVPs) that are sent in the clear, but some payloads, such as network keys and private identifiers, need to be delivered privately.
tldr.mechanism: Two new AVPs negotiate an encryption algorithm and wrap the AVPs to protect inside one Encryption-Encap AVP, encrypted with AES-128 in counter mode under keys derived from the EAP master session key.
tldr.outcome: Specifications for AVPs can now mark each one as must-encrypt, must-not-encrypt or optional. RFC 6786 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 6786 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PANA Needs Encryption
sections.content:
PANA, defined in RFC 5191, is a UDP-based protocol that runs an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) exchange between a PANA Client (PaC) and a PANA Authentication Agent (PAA). Its payloads travel in Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs).

AVPs can be integrity protected with the AUTH AVP when the EAP method generates cryptographic keying material, but they are sent unencrypted. Some payloads, for example network keys and private identifiers, need to be delivered privately. RFC 6786 defines a way to encrypt selected AVPs.
sections.eli5: PANA messages are like postcards anyone can read. Some things written on them are secrets, so we need a way to hide just those parts.

sections.title: Negotiating the Algorithm
sections.content:
RFC 6786 adds two AVPs to the set in RFC 5191: the Encryption-Algorithm AVP and the Encryption-Encap AVP. It also defines two new keys, PANA_PAC_ENCR_KEY for traffic from the PaC to the PAA and PANA_PAA_ENCR_KEY for traffic from the PAA to the PaC.

When encryption is needed, the PAA MUST send the initial PANA-Auth-Request carrying one or more Encryption-Algorithm AVPs that it supports. The PaC MUST pick one and answer with the initial PANA-Auth-Answer carrying one Encryption-Algorithm AVP for its choice. Once both keys exist, a PANA message MAY contain an Encryption-Encap AVP.

The Encryption-Algorithm AVP has AVP code 13 and an Unsigned32 value. Only AES128_CTR (value 1) is defined here. Other values are reserved for future specifications, and unless an application profile says otherwise, all implementations MUST support AES128_CTR.
sections.eli5: First the two sides agree on which secret code to use. One offers a list, and the other picks one from it.

sections.title: The Encryption Keys
sections.content:
Each key is computed with the prf+ function from the Internet Key Exchange protocol version 2, keyed with the master session key (MSK) from the EAP method. The inputs are a label ("IETF PANA PaC Encr" or "IETF PANA PAA Encr"), the initial PANA-Auth-Request and PANA-Auth-Answer messages, the PaC and PAA nonces, and the value of the Key-Id AVP.

The pseudo-random function used inside prf+ is the one negotiated with the PRF-Algorithm AVP in the initial exchange. The keys MUST be recalculated whenever the EAP method generates a new MSK, and their length depends on the encryption algorithm in use.

The keys are secret and shared between the PaC and the PAA. They MUST NOT be used for anything other than what this document specifies.
sections.eli5: Both sides take a shared secret they already have and mix it with some one-time numbers to make two fresh keys, one for each direction.

sections.title: AES128_CTR Encryption
sections.content:
AES128_CTR uses the AES-CTR (counter) mode of operation from NIST SP 800-38A with the AES-128 block cipher. The formatting and counter generation functions come from Appendix A of NIST SP 800-38C, with n = 12 and q = 3.

The 12-octet nonce is made of a 4-octet Key-Id, a 4-octet Session ID and a 4-octet Sequence Number, in that order, each in network byte order. The Session ID and Sequence Number are the same as in the PANA message that carries the Encryption-Encap AVP. The RFC works through an example in which Key-Id 0x55667788, Session ID 0xaabbccdd and Sequence Number 0x11223344 give a first counter block of 0x0255667788aabbccdd11223344000001.

The nonce is unique per key as long as the sequence number does not wrap. If a sender is about to wrap the sequence number, the PaC (for traffic to the PAA) or the PAA (for traffic to the PaC) MUST start PANA re-authentication, which produces a new MSK and therefore new keys.
sections.eli5: The scrambler uses a counter that goes up each time, so no two messages are ever scrambled the same way. Before the counter runs out, the two sides start over with new keys.

sections.title: The Encryption-Encap AVP
sections.content:
The Encryption-Encap AVP (AVP code 12) holds one or more encrypted PANA AVPs. With AES128_CTR, its data payload is the encrypted AVPs. A PANA message SHALL contain only one Encryption-Encap AVP, and every AVP that needs encryption SHALL go inside it.

It SHALL be used only if the EAP method generates cryptographic keys. The PaC MAY use it once PANA_PAC_ENCR_KEY exists, and the PAA MAY use it once PANA_PAA_ENCR_KEY exists, after the algorithm has been negotiated. It MAY appear in the very first message carrying the Result-Code AVP set to PANA_Success, and in any later message of the same PANA session.
sections.eli5: The Encryption-Encap AVP is the locked envelope. Everything secret goes inside one envelope, and only one envelope is allowed per message.

sections.title: Encryption Policy for AVPs
sections.content:
The specification of any AVP SHOULD say whether the AVP shall or shall not be encrypted with Encryption-Encap, using a table with three symbols. If a specification is silent, the AVP MAY be encrypted.

  • Y: the AVP SHALL be encrypted. If it arrives unencrypted it is invalid and the message is discarded.
  • N: the AVP SHALL NOT be encrypted. If it arrives encrypted it is invalid and the message is discarded.
  • X: the AVP MAY be encrypted, and either form is valid.

Guidance: use Y if the payload needs privacy against eavesdroppers (for example a secret key), N if on-path network elements may need to see it, and X if neither applies. For the existing AVPs, the RFC marks EAP-Payload, Session-Lifetime and Termination-Cause as X. AUTH, Integrity-Algorithm, Key-Id, Nonce, PRF-Algorithm and Result-Code are N, as are PaC-Information, Relayed-Message and the two new AVPs.
sections.eli5: Every kind of note gets a rule: always lock it, never lock it, or either way is fine. If the rule is broken, the message is thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Compromise of PANA_PAC_ENCR_KEY or PANA_PAA_ENCR_KEY would compromise the secret information they protect, which is why they SHALL NOT be reused for other purposes.

AES-CTR has its own considerations, listed in RFC 3686. The nonce meets the uniqueness-per-key requirement. AES-CTR also needs a companion authentication function, and this is met because, once the EAP method has generated keys, an AUTH AVP is present in every PANA message, so an Encryption-Encap AVP always travels with an AUTH AVP.
sections.eli5: If someone steals the keys, they can read the secrets, so the keys must be used only for this job. Each locked message also carries a signature that shows nobody tampered with it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered standard AVP code 12 for Encryption-Encap and code 13 for Encryption-Algorithm. In the new Encryption-Algorithm sub-registry, value 1 is AES128_CTR and the other values (0, 2-4294967295) are unassigned. New values need IETF Review or IESG Approval.

An "Enc" column holding the policy from the previous section was also added to the "AVP Codes" sub-registry and filled in for all existing AVP codes and the ones defined here.
sections.eli5: The official list of PANA codes got two new entries and a new column telling which items get locked.

messages.label: PANA-Auth-Request (initial)
messages.note: Carries one or more Encryption-Algorithm AVPs the PAA supports.

messages.label: PANA-Auth-Answer (initial)
messages.note: Carries one Encryption-Algorithm AVP for the selected algorithm.

items.label: Must encrypt
items.desc: Unencrypted AVP is invalid; message is discarded.

items.label: Must not encrypt
items.desc: Encrypted AVP is invalid; message is discarded.
